description: Question: transistors kept doubling for fifty years, so why did clock speed stop rising around 2005, and where did the extra transistors go? Data: Karl Rupp's microprocessor trend data (CC BY 4.0; transistors, clock, typical power, single-thread SpecINT and logical cores for about 100 CPUs, 1971–2021). Steps: each measure as log2 of its value against year, so a straight line is a constant doubling time; for the clock, a two-line fit for every candidate break year from 1995 to 2014 (the year with the smallest squared error wins); each measure fitted before and after that year with 95% intervals; a Chow F-test of one line against two; and Dennard's budget: dynamic power P ≈ N·C·V²·f, so the doublings per year of transistors × clock minus those of power is how fast the switching energy C·V² had to fall. Aha: the transistor line barely bends at the break, but the clock and power lines go flat: until the mid-2000s each shrink lowered the voltage, paying for faster clocks at constant power density (Dennard scaling); when leakage stopped the voltage from falling, the clock froze at the cooling limit and the extra transistors became cores. Caveats: points before 2010 were digitised from a published plot (Horowitz, Labonte, Shacham, Olukotun, Hammond, Batten), later ones collected by Rupp; the sample is high-end Intel/AMD/IBM CPUs, not phones or GPUs; power is TDP; the break year is chosen on the clock data, so the clock's Chow p-value is optimistic; each file's first line (the 1971 Intel 4004) is read as a CSV header and dropped. Next: the voltage data that would test the mechanism (in the study), die area for power density, and Rupp's blog post for the story.
name: Moore's law and the end of Dennard scaling
